title: Crows can evaluate visual info twice as fast as mammals
gist: A Science study by Andreas Nieder and Philipp Schmidbauer (University of Tübingen) ran two carrion crows through the primate random-dot-motion task: the crows matched monkey and human accuracy but decided in about 235 ms versus roughly 410-600 ms for monkeys. Recordings from 248 NCL neurons show the same evidence-accumulating decision variable seen in the primate neocortex, which Nieder reads as evolution finding the same mechanism twice; he attributes the speed to small neurons with short axons and high body temperature, with caveats about the two-bird sample.

themes.theme: Crows match primate accuracy at twice the speed

insights.claim: In a random-dot-motion task, two carrion crows averaged 235 milliseconds from the dots appearing to starting their peck, while monkeys in closely matched versions of the task took roughly 410, 490 and 600 milliseconds across three studies.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark showing that a non-layered neural architecture can make perceptual decisions faster than primate cortex.
insights.locator: Measured from the moment that the dots appeared

insights.claim: The crows' speed did not come from trading away accuracy: they were as accurate as monkeys or humans on the same task, and both birds beat chance even when only 3 percent of the dots moved coherently.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Rules out the simple speed-accuracy tradeoff explanation, so the speed gain is a real processing advantage.
insights.quote: This would be a simple explanation, that they are very fast at the cost of precision. But that’s not what’s happening

insights.claim: The crows were never pushed to respond quickly; under self-paced decisions they were still about twice as fast as any monkey or human Nieder knows of.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Shows the speed is the birds' default operating point, not a trained artifact.
insights.quote: We just gave them a self-paced decision. And even in this situation, they were twice as fast compared to any monkey or human that I’m aware of.

insights.claim: Task difficulty barely changed crow reaction times, which ran from 220 ms on the easiest condition to 254 ms on the hardest, a 34 ms spread, whereas in primates difficulty strongly lengthens decisions.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: The flat difficulty curve initially suggested a fixed-deadline mechanism, which matters for how avian decision circuits are modeled.
insights.locator: One possible reason for the crows’ speed

themes.theme: Same decision variable in a different brain

insights.claim: Nieder argues that crows do accumulate evidence rather than answering on a timer, because zooming in shows reaction time rising statistically as coherence falls, the same effect as in mammals but much smaller because everything runs faster.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Supports the idea that one computational principle (evidence accumulation) carries across very different neural hardware.
insights.quote: If you zoom in, there is a statistical increase in the reaction time when the coherence is going down

insights.claim: 58 of the 248 recorded NCL neurons fired differently depending on which direction the crow would choose, and they began signaling that choice about 70 ms after the dots appeared, roughly 170 ms before the head moved.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Gives a precise neural timeline for avian decisions, useful to anyone comparing biological and artificial decision architectures.

insights.claim: Because the crow NCL produces a decision variable that looks basically the same as the one in monkey neocortex despite separately evolved brains, Nieder concludes evolution found the same physiological mechanism twice, independently.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Convergent evolution of the same computation suggests evidence accumulation is a robust general solution for decision-making.
insights.quote: as if evolution has found the same physiological mechanism twice, independently
insights.locator: This kind of signal in the brain

insights.claim: Birds and mammals split more than 360 million years ago: mammalian cortex is stacked layers of cells, while the bird equivalent (including the NCL, the functional counterpart of primate prefrontal cortex) is dense clusters with no layering, and the study found this alternative architecture proved faster.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Evidence that layered cortex is not the only or fastest design for high-level cognition.
insights.locator: Birds and mammals parted evolutionary ways

insights.claim: Nieder cannot pin the speed on one fast process and instead suggests a cascade of faster steps, starting with highly movement-sensitive avian vision and extending through the decision to the motor response.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Speed comes from the whole pipeline being faster, not from one specialized module.
insights.quote: It is probably a cascade of different processes that are faster
insights.locator: We cannot really point our finger

insights.claim: Flight's weight limits push birds to pack many very small neurons into small brains with shorter axons, which Nieder says speeds signaling because long lines take time.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Physical compactness as a driver of computational speed is a familiar principle in chip design too.
insights.quote: Long lines take time. Short lines speed everything up

insights.claim: Bird body temperatures of 41 to 42 degrees Celsius, versus about 36.6 in humans, speed up all chemical processes, so ion channels and synaptic transmitters work faster.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A second physical mechanism behind avian speed, framed by Nieder as evolution pushing bird bodies to the limit.
insights.quote: Every ion channel would open and close faster. Every transmitter would move through the synaptic cleft faster

insights.claim: The study used only two crows; Nieder concedes this is a valid limit but notes two animals is the standard for complex combined behavior-and-electrophysiology monkey studies.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A small sample means the speed claim needs replication before it is treated as general.
insights.locator: First, the study included only two birds

insights.claim: The 235 ms crow and 400+ ms primate times are specific to the random-dot task, which by design requires waiting to see the drift, so they are not absolute limits on decision speed.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: The numbers are task-relative comparisons, not universal speed limits.

insights.claim: It is unclear whether the results reflect fast bird brains in general or the intelligence of corvids specifically, because most other birds are not smart enough to be trained on this task.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Limits how far the finding can be generalized across birds.
insights.quote: you need a smart bird in order to train it to do exactly this task
